blocks.text: Von Willebrand disease (VWD) is an inherited bleeding disorder caused by **too little von Willebrand factor (vWF) or vWF that does not work properly**. Types 1 and 3 are **quantitative** defects and type 2 is **qualitative**. vWF both anchors platelets to damaged vessel wall and carries factor VIII, so its loss gives a **combined defect**: poor platelet plug formation plus a secondary fall in factor VIII.

blocks.title: How common is it?
items: Overall, the **commonest inherited bleeding disorder**; haemophilia A and B lead only among _single coagulation factor_ deficiencies
Prevalence about **1% of the population** (First Aid); Step-Up quotes **1–3%**
Type mix: about **85% type 1**, about **15% type 2**, and **under 1% type 3**
Usually mild, so many people are only diagnosed after unexpected bleeding with surgery or trauma

blocks.title: Genetics to remember
items: The vWF gene sits on **chromosome 12**, so VWD is **autosomal**
It therefore affects **both sexes**, unlike the **X-linked** haemophilias A and B
**Variable penetrance**: within one family some members bleed often and badly while others have almost no symptoms
Type 3 is recessive, so the patient's **parents are often clinically normal** carriers

blocks.text: Quick sources (First Aid) simplify this to "types 1 and 2 dominant, type 3 recessive". Davidson's is more precise: **type 2N is also autosomal recessive**, alongside type 3. Use the Davidson version in the exam.
Exam clue: **male-to-male transmission** (an affected father and son) or **symptomatic women in several generations** points to an **autosomal** disorder such as VWD, not X-linked haemophilia.

sections.title: Pathogenesis: what von Willebrand factor does

blocks.text: vWF is a large glycoprotein made by **endothelial cells and megakaryocytes**. It circulates as **multimers**; the multimeric structure is what lets it grip subendothelial collagen and platelets. Factor VIII coagulant protein, by contrast, is made mainly in the **liver** (and endothelium).

blocks.title: The two jobs of vWF
items: **Platelet adhesion ("platelet glue")**: vWF bridges exposed subendothelium (e.g. collagen) and the platelet receptor **GPIb (GPIb/V/IX complex)**, so platelets stick to a damaged vessel; it also helps platelets aggregate
**Carrier for factor VIII**: vWF binds factor VIII non-covalently and **shields it from proteolysis**; factor VIII has a half-life of only about 12 hours and relies on vWF to escape early breakdown

blocks.text: So vWF deficiency causes a **dual haemostatic defect**: a weak platelet plug (mucosal bleeding, prolonged bleeding time) and a **reduced factor VIII level**, which can lengthen the APTT when the fall is large.

blocks.title: vWF versus factor VIII coagulant protein
rows: Platelet adhesion; carries and protects FVIII

blocks.text: vWF carries the **A and B blood group antigens**, which slow its breakdown. People who are **blood group O** therefore have **lower vWF levels** than non-O people — keep this in mind before labelling someone with VWD.

Older terminology calls vWF **"factor VIII-related antigen"** (the antigenic part of the circulating factor VIII complex). It is a **different protein** from factor VIII coagulant, which is the one missing in haemophilia A.

blocks.note: Look at: the stages of normal haemostasis — GPIa on collagen, GPIb on vWF and GPIIb/IIIa on fibrinogen, then fibrin clot.
Look at: the platelet surface glycoproteins — GPIb/V/IX is the vWF receptor; also note GPIIb/IIIa and the alpha and dense granules.

blocks.text: VWD bleeds like a **platelet function disorder**: superficial, **mucocutaneous** bleeding. Episodes are **far less frequent than in severe haemophilia**, and in many patients abnormal bleeding shows up only after **trauma, surgery or a dental extraction**.

blocks.title: Typical history
items: Easy **bruising** and prolonged bleeding from small cuts
**Epistaxis** and **bleeding gums** on brushing
**Menorrhagia** — affects more than half of menstruating patients
Prolonged bleeding after **dental extraction** or surgery
**Gastrointestinal bleeding** can occur but is less common
Often starts in **childhood**, with a **positive family history**; symptoms **worsen with aspirin**

blocks.title: Two patterns of bleeding
rows: Deep tissues: joints, muscles, retroperitoneum, brain
Bleeding is **delayed** and can be severe

blocks.title: Severity by type
items: **Types 1 and 2**: usually mild — bleeding after minor trauma or surgery, epistaxis, menorrhagia; **haemarthroses are rare**
**Type 3**: more severe bleeding, yet joint and muscle bleeds like those of haemophilia are still uncommon

blocks.text: **Dental extraction, tonsillectomy and circumcision** act as natural "stress tests" of haemostasis. Ask about them: **immediate** bleeding points to a platelet-plug (primary haemostasis) problem such as VWD; **delayed** bleeding points to a coagulation defect.

**Spontaneous haemarthroses do not fit ordinary VWD.** A boy with a hot swollen knee after trivial trauma has haemophilia until proven otherwise; recurrent nosebleeds and heavy periods in a woman suggest VWD.

Three main types: **type 1** (partial quantitative deficiency of normal vWF — the commonest), **type 2** (qualitatively abnormal vWF, with several subtypes) and **type 3** (virtually complete absence — the rarest and most severe). The type 2 subtypes depend on where the mutation affects binding to platelets, collagen or factor VIII.

blocks.title: Types of VWD and their laboratory patterns
rows: vWF antigen, ristocetin cofactor activity and FVIII:C all fall **in parallel**
HMW multimers reduced; **enhanced RIPA**; may cause thrombocytopenia
Very low vWF and FVIII:C; **multimers absent**

blocks.title: Memory hooks for type 2
items: **2A** — large multimers **A**bsent
**2B** — **B**inds platelets too avidly, so platelets are cleared (low count) and RIPA is enhanced
**2M** — **M**ultimers normal, but platelet binding is faulty
**2N** — the problem is the factor VIII binding site, so the standout result is a **low FVIII**

blocks.title: Acquired von Willebrand syndrome
items: **Immune-mediated** (anti-vWF antibodies)
Associated with **Wilms' tumour**, other malignancy, **myeloproliferative neoplasms with a high platelet count**, autoimmune disease, **hypothyroidism** and drugs
Mechanisms: antibodies, increased clearance or reduced synthesis of vWF
**Heyde syndrome**: severe **aortic stenosis** + **GI bleeding** (angiodysplasia/AVMs) + acquired VWD — high shear across the valve cleaves and destroys vWF

blocks.text: An elderly patient with an **ejection systolic murmur** and **recurrent GI bleeding** with no personal history of bleeding: think **Heyde syndrome** (acquired VWD from aortic stenosis).

blocks.title: Typical screening results in VWD
items: **Platelet count normal** (except type 2B, which can lower it)
**PT normal**
**APTT normal or prolonged** — it lengthens only when factor VIII is low enough
Bleeding time prolonged (classic teaching; the test itself is now rarely used)

blocks.title: Specific tests
items: **vWF antigen** (vWF:Ag) — low
**vWF activity** by the **ristocetin cofactor assay** (vWF-dependent platelet agglutination) — low; quick sources call it the best initial specific test
**Factor VIII:C** — low (useful but less specific)
**Multimer analysis** — confirms and types the disease
**RIPA** (tests GPIb binding, enhanced in 2B) and **vWF–FVIII binding assay** (for 2N)
**vWF gene mutation analysis** is informative in most cases

blocks.text: **A normal APTT does not exclude VWD**, and routine screening tests often miss it. If the history strongly suggests a bleeding disorder but the screen is normal, go on to **vWF assays and platelet function tests**.

Kumar's table lists a **prolonged APTT** for VWD, while Davidson's stresses that the APTT **can be normal**. Both fit: the APTT tracks the factor VIII level. Davidson's also notes that most centres have **abandoned the bleeding time** in favour of in-vitro platelet aggregation and ristocetin agglutination tests.

blocks.title: Differential diagnosis
columns: Clues that separate it from VWD
rows: Males; joint and muscle bleeds; APTT markedly prolonged; **vWF normal**, FVIII very low
Clinically like A; low factor IX; vWF normal
**Giant platelets** and mild thrombocytopenia on the film
Normal platelet count and morphology; often severe bleeding
Low platelet count; film otherwise normal
Low platelets with prolonged PT and APTT; acutely unwell

blocks.text: The **ristocetin cofactor assay** separates VWD from other platelet disorders such as Bernard–Soulier syndrome: in VWD the defect is in the patient's **plasma vWF**, whereas in Bernard–Soulier the **platelet receptor** (GPIb-IX) is missing.

**TTP is the opposite vWF problem.** Lack of ADAMTS13, the vWF-cleaving protease, leaves **ultralarge vWF multimers** that form microthrombi, consume platelets and cause microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia — thrombosis, not a VWD-type bleeding tendency.

blocks.title: Complications
items: **Excessive bleeding after surgery or trauma**, especially when the diagnosis is not yet known
**Thrombocytopenia in type 2B**, which can become troublesome after desmopressin
Treatment-related: desmopressin **hyponatraemia** (fits in young children) and **arterial thrombosis**; infection risk from pooled plasma products (see Management)

blocks.note: Look at: normal FVIII–vWF synthesis versus haemophilia A (X-chromosome FVIII gene defect) and VWD (reduced endothelial vWF synthesis, so FVIII is left unprotected).

blocks.text: Most patients need **no regular daily treatment**. Treatment is given to **stop a significant bleed** or to **cover surgery and dental procedures**. All patients should **avoid aspirin, NSAIDs and other antiplatelet drugs**, and intramuscular injections.

blocks.title: Treatment options
rows: Releases stored vWF from endothelium; raises vWF and FVIII **3–4-fold**
Hyponatraemia; avoid in young children and severe arterial disease; tachyphylaxis; type 2B thrombocytopenia; **useless in type 3**
FVIII concentrate rich in vWF (plasma-derived) or recombinant vWF
Pooled plasma product (vaccinate against hepatitis A and B)
Only if virus-inactivated or recombinant products are unavailable

blocks.title: Desmopressin: exam facts
items: Haemostatic dose about **0.3 μg/kg IV or SC** — higher than the dose for diabetes insipidus; **300 μg intranasally** gives a similar effect
Repeated doses cause **water retention** → monitor sodium for **hyponatraemia**
**Tachyphylaxis**: it works for only about **3–5 days** of repeated use
Check the patient's response with a **trial dose** before relying on it for a procedure

blocks.title: Heavy menstrual bleeding in VWD
items: **Tranexamic acid** or **mefenamic acid**
Hormonal control: **combined oral contraceptive pill**, norethisterone, or a **levonorgestrel IUS (Mirena)**
**Hysterectomy** in severe, refractory cases

blocks.text: **Desmopressin in type 2 — sources differ.** Step-Up calls it less effective, Pocket Medicine says avoid it in type 2, and First Aid treats type 2 as non-responders. Davidson's singles out **type 2B**, where it can cause troublesome **thrombocytopenia**, and says **type 3 responds only to FVIII/vWF concentrate**. Safe exam answer: desmopressin for type 1; concentrate for type 3, major bleeds and surgery.

Not every factor VIII product will do: choose a **concentrate that contains plenty of vWF** (high-molecular-weight vWF). Cryoprecipitate contains vWF but is a last resort because it is not virus-inactivated.
Anyone likely to receive **pooled plasma products** who is not immune should be offered **hepatitis A and B vaccination**.

cards.back: **Von Willebrand disease** — about 1% of people (quoted range 1–3%).
Mostly **autosomal dominant** (1, 2A, 2B, 2M); **2N and 3 are autosomal recessive**. vWF gene on **chromosome 12**.

cards.front: Approximate share of VWD types 1, 2 and 3?

cards.back: 1) **Platelet adhesion** — bridges subendothelium to platelet **GPIb**. 2) **Carries and protects factor VIII** from proteolysis.
**Endothelial cells and megakaryocytes** (factor VIII coagulant is made mainly by the liver).

cards.front: Why do blood group O people have lower vWF?
cards.back: A and B antigens on vWF slow its proteolysis; group O vWF lacks them, so levels run lower — a diagnostic trap.
**Mucocutaneous**: bruising, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, bleeding after dental extraction or surgery. Haemarthroses are rare.

cards.front: Immediate versus delayed bleeding after surgery?
cards.back: **Immediate** → platelet plug / primary haemostasis defect (e.g. VWD). **Delayed** → coagulation factor defect.
Increased vWF affinity for **GPIb**; reduced HMW multimers; **enhanced RIPA**; **thrombocytopenia** (worse after desmopressin).
Mutation in vWF's **factor VIII binding site** → **low FVIII**; **autosomal recessive**.
**Aortic stenosis + GI bleeding + acquired VWD** — shear stress across the valve cleaves vWF.

cards.front: Classic lab pattern: VWD versus haemophilia A?
cards.back: VWD: bleeding time ↑, PT normal, APTT ↑ (or normal), FVIII ↓, **vWF ↓**. Haemophilia A: bleeding time normal, APTT ↑↑, FVIII ↓↓, **vWF normal**.

cards.front: Does a normal APTT exclude VWD?
cards.back: **No.** The APTT is prolonged only when FVIII is low enough. Measure vWF if the history is suggestive.

cards.front: How does desmopressin help in VWD?
cards.back: Releases stored vWF from endothelium → vWF and FVIII rise **3–4-fold**. Best for **type 1**; useless in type 3.
**Hyponatraemia** (fits in young children), **thrombosis** in severe arterial disease, **tachyphylaxis** after 3–5 days, **thrombocytopenia in type 2B**.

cards.front: Treatment of bleeding in type 3 VWD?
cards.back: **vWF-containing factor VIII concentrate** (or recombinant vWF) — desmopressin does not work.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman has had heavy periods since menarche and frequent nosebleeds. Her father bled for two days after a dental extraction, and her brother bruises easily.
questions.leadIn: Which mode of inheritance best explains this family history?
questions.explanation: Bleeding in **both sexes across successive generations**, with an affected father and an affected son, fits **autosomal dominant** inheritance — the usual pattern for von Willebrand disease (vWF gene on chromosome 12).
whyNot: Recessive disease usually skips generations and the parents are typically unaffected carriers; here the father is affected.
X-linked recessive disease (haemophilia) is passed from carrier mothers to sons; an affected father cannot pass an X-linked gene to his son.
An X-linked dominant gene from an affected father goes to all daughters but no sons, yet the brother is affected.
Mitochondrial genes pass only through the mother, but here the father is the affected parent.

questions.stem: A medical student is revising inherited bleeding disorders for a viva.
questions.leadIn: Which statement about von Willebrand disease is correct?
options: It is the most common inherited bleeding disorder
It is less common than haemophilia A
Type 2 accounts for about 85% of cases
questions.explanation: VWD is the **commonest inherited bleeding disorder** (about 1% of people). Type 1 makes up about 85% of cases, type 2 about 15% and type 3 under 1%.
whyNot: Haemophilia A is the commonest single coagulation factor deficiency, but VWD is more common overall.
Type 3 is the rarest type (under 1%).
VWD is autosomal, so both sexes are affected.
About 85% is the share of type 1; type 2 is roughly 15%.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl with easy bruising has a low von Willebrand factor antigen level. Her factor VIII coagulant activity is also reduced, although her factor VIII gene is normal.
questions.leadIn: What best explains the low factor VIII level?
options: vWF normally protects factor VIII from proteolysis
vWF is needed for hepatic synthesis of factor VIII
vWF converts factor VIII to its active form
Antibodies against factor VIII have formed
Factor VIII is consumed in platelet aggregates
questions.explanation: vWF is the **carrier protein** for factor VIII and shields it from breakdown. When vWF is low, unprotected factor VIII is cleared early, so its plasma level falls — the coagulation half of VWD's dual defect.
whyNot: Factor VIII is made normally (mainly by the liver); the problem is its survival in plasma, not its synthesis.
vWF does not activate factor VIII; its job is to carry it and protect it from breakdown.
An inhibitor would be acquired, typically after factor VIII therapy, and is not the explanation in a child with low vWF.
Consumption of factors occurs in DIC, not in VWD.

questions.stem: During a haematology tutorial, students label a diagram of the platelet surface and the steps of platelet adhesion to injured endothelium.
questions.leadIn: Which platelet receptor binds von Willebrand factor?
questions.explanation: Platelets adhere when **GPIb (the GPIb/V/IX complex)** binds vWF that is attached to exposed subendothelium. GPIIb/IIIa then mediates aggregation via fibrinogen.
whyNot: GPIIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen and mediates aggregation; it is missing in Glanzmann thrombasthenia.
GPIa binds collagen directly, not vWF.
GPVI is another surface glycoprotein shown on the diagram, but the vWF receptor is GPIb/V/IX.
ADP is a soluble agonist that activates platelets; its receptor does not bind vWF.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is assessed for a possible lifelong bleeding tendency before elective surgery.
questions.leadIn: Which feature of his history would most suggest a defect of primary haemostasis (platelets or vWF) rather than a coagulation factor deficiency?
options: Bleeding that began immediately after a dental extraction
A calf haematoma causing compartment syndrome
Bleeding that restarted a day after tonsillectomy
A retroperitoneal haemorrhage after minor trauma
questions.explanation: **Immediate** post-procedure bleeding reflects a failure to form the platelet plug — the pattern seen in VWD and platelet disorders. Deep tissue bleeds and **delayed** bleeding point to coagulation factor deficiency.
whyNot: Haemarthrosis is the hallmark of a coagulation factor deficiency such as haemophilia.
Muscle haematomas are deep tissue bleeds typical of haemophilia.
Delayed bleeding after surgery suggests a coagulation defect.
Retroperitoneal bleeding is a deep bleed of coagulation factor deficiency.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl has had very heavy periods since menarche 2 years ago, with easy bruising and gum bleeding on brushing. Her father had prolonged bleeding after a tonsillectomy. Platelet count is 260 × 10⁹/L, the blood film is normal and the PT is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Mucocutaneous bleeding from childhood, **menorrhagia**, a **normal platelet count and film**, and an **affected father** (autosomal dominant) make **VWD** most likely.
whyNot: Haemophilia A is X-linked, so girls are rarely affected, and its typical bleeds are into joints and muscles rather than mucosa.
ITP causes a low platelet count, but her count is normal.
Glanzmann thrombasthenia is autosomal recessive, so an affected parent would be unusual.
Bernard–Soulier shows giant platelets and mild thrombocytopenia on the film, and is autosomal recessive.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with mild mucosal bleeding has vWF antigen, ristocetin cofactor activity and factor VIII:C all reduced to around 35–40% of normal. The activity-to-antigen ratio is close to 1 and multimer analysis shows a normal distribution.
questions.leadIn: Which type of von Willebrand disease is most likely?
questions.explanation: **Parallel reduction** of antigen, activity and factor VIII with **normal multimers** means less vWF of normal quality — **type 1**, a partial quantitative defect and the commonest type.
whyNot: Type 2A lacks HMW multimers and has an activity:antigen ratio below 0.7.
Type 2B has reduced HMW multimers and enhanced RIPA, often with thrombocytopenia.
Type 2N mainly lowers factor VIII because vWF cannot bind it; antigen and activity are not reduced in parallel.
Type 3 shows very low vWF and FVIII with absent multimers and severe bleeding.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with von Willebrand disease is given desmopressin before a dental procedure. Next day his platelet count has fallen from 140 to 60 × 10⁹/L. Earlier tests showed reduced high-molecular-weight multimers and enhanced ristocetin-induced platelet agglutination.
questions.leadIn: Which type of von Willebrand disease does he have?
questions.explanation: Type **2B** vWF binds platelet GPIb **too avidly**, giving **enhanced RIPA**, loss of HMW multimers and **thrombocytopenia**, which can become troublesome after desmopressin.
whyNot: Type 1 shows parallel falls with normal multimers and no enhanced RIPA.
Type 2A lacks HMW multimers, but RIPA is not enhanced and thrombocytopenia is not a feature.
Type 2M has normal multimers.
Type 3 has absent multimers and does not respond to desmopressin at all.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has recurrent nosebleeds and heavy periods. Her mother has similar symptoms. Her platelet count is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which set of results is most likely?
options: Bleeding time ↑, PT normal, APTT ↑, FVIII:C ↓, vWF ↓
Bleeding time normal, PT normal, APTT ↑↑, FVIII:C ↓↓, vWF normal
Bleeding time normal, PT ↑, APTT ↑, FVIII:C normal, vWF normal
Bleeding time ↑, giant platelets, mild thrombocytopenia, vWF normal
PT ↑ and APTT ↑ with thrombocytopenia and raised D-dimer
questions.explanation: This is likely VWD. The classic pattern is **prolonged bleeding time** (platelet adhesion defect), **normal PT**, an APTT that is prolonged if FVIII is low enough, **reduced FVIII:C** and **reduced vWF**.
whyNot: This is the haemophilia A pattern: an isolated, marked APTT prolongation with normal vWF.
Prolonged PT and APTT with normal FVIII and vWF fits vitamin K deficiency.
Giant platelets with mild thrombocytopenia suggest Bernard–Soulier syndrome; her platelet count is normal.
Prolonged PT and APTT with low platelets suggest DIC in an acutely unwell patient.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman has a convincing history of heavy periods, nosebleeds and prolonged bleeding after a wisdom tooth extraction. Her platelet count, PT and APTT are all normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Measure vWF antigen, vWF activity and factor VIII
Reassure her that a bleeding disorder is excluded
questions.explanation: Screening tests **do not reliably detect VWD**, and the APTT can be normal. With a strongly suggestive history, go on to **specific vWF assays** (and platelet function testing).
whyNot: A normal screen does not exclude VWD; Davidson's warns against relying on it.
Bone marrow examination is not part of the work-up of a normal platelet count with mucosal bleeding.
Factor IX deficiency (haemophilia B) is X-linked and prolongs the APTT; it is not the next step here.
A mixing study is used to investigate a prolonged PT or APTT; her clotting times are normal.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with known type 1 von Willebrand disease needs a dental extraction. A previous trial dose of desmopressin raised his vWF and factor VIII levels well.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate haemostatic plan?
questions.explanation: In **type 1** VWD with a proven response, **desmopressin** (releases stored vWF; raises vWF and FVIII 3–4-fold) covers minor procedures. **Tranexamic acid** helps mucosal bleeding such as in the mouth.
whyNot: Platelet numbers are normal in type 1 VWD; the defect is in vWF.
Plasma is not used when a proven desmopressin response or specific concentrates are available.
Recombinant VIIa is used for resistant bleeding in Glanzmann thrombasthenia, not routine VWD cover.
IV immunoglobulin treats immune thrombocytopenia, not VWD.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with type 3 von Willebrand disease is scheduled for a hip replacement.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate haemostatic cover?
options: Plasma-derived factor VIII concentrate containing vWF
questions.explanation: Type 3 has virtually **no vWF**, so there is nothing for desmopressin to release. Bleeding responds only to **factor VIII/vWF concentrate** (or recombinant vWF), which is also the cover for major surgery.
whyNot: Desmopressin works by releasing stored vWF and is ineffective in type 3.
Tranexamic acid is only an adjunct for mucosal bleeding and cannot cover major surgery alone.
Cryoprecipitate is not virus-inactivated and is a last resort when concentrates are unavailable.
The platelet count is normal; the deficiency is of vWF and FVIII.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: An 8-year-old boy has a hot, swollen knee after a minor fall and had a large thigh haematoma last year. His maternal uncle has a similar problem. APTT is prolonged, PT is normal, factor VIII is very low and vWF is normal.
items.explanation: Joint and muscle bleeds in a boy with **maternal-line** inheritance, low FVIII and **normal vWF** mean **haemophilia A**.

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman has recurrent nosebleeds and heavy periods; her father has similar symptoms. Platelet count is normal. vWF antigen and ristocetin cofactor activity are both about 40% of normal and multimers are normal.
items.explanation: Parallel moderate reduction with normal multimers and autosomal dominant spread is **type 1 VWD**.

items.stem: A 6-year-old girl has severe nosebleeds and one episode of gastrointestinal bleeding. Her parents are first cousins and neither has any bleeding problem. vWF is undetectable and factor VIII:C is very low.
items.explanation: Two steps: consanguineous, **unaffected parents** suggest **autosomal recessive** inheritance, and **absent vWF** with very low FVIII marks the severe quantitative form — **type 3 VWD**.

items.stem: A 17-year-old boy whose parents are healthy has lifelong mucosal bleeding. His platelet count is 90 × 10⁹/L and the film shows giant platelets. vWF levels are normal.
items.explanation: Giant platelets with mild thrombocytopenia and normal vWF point to **Bernard–Soulier syndrome** — absent GPIb-IX, the platelet receptor for vWF.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Low vWF explained by blood group O (not VWD)

items.stem: A 29-year-old man has epistaxis. vWF antigen is mildly low, but ristocetin cofactor activity is much lower (activity:antigen ratio 0.4). High-molecular-weight multimers are absent.
items.explanation: Absent HMW multimers with an activity:antigen ratio **below 0.7** is **type 2A**.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman has a low factor VIII:C level but normal vWF antigen and activity. Her parents are unaffected. In a binding assay, her vWF fails to bind factor VIII.
items.explanation: Two steps: the isolated low FVIII comes from **defective vWF–FVIII binding**, and unaffected parents fit **autosomal recessive** inheritance — **type 2N**.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman has a bleeding history. Her vWF platelet-binding activity is far lower than her antigen level (activity:antigen ratio 0.3), but multimer analysis shows a completely normal pattern.
items.explanation: A ratio **well below 0.7** shows abnormal platelet binding; with **normal multimers** this is **type 2M** (type 2A would lack HMW multimers).

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman with no personal or family bleeding history has a borderline-low vWF level on routine pre-operative testing. She is blood group O.
items.explanation: Blood group O lowers vWF in healthy people because vWF lacks the protective A and B antigens. This must be considered before diagnosing VWD.

questions.leadIn: For each scenario below, choose the single most useful next investigation from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Platelet aggregation with ADP and collagen

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman with mucosal bleeding has low vWF antigen and an even lower ristocetin cofactor activity (activity:antigen ratio 0.5). The team now wants to see the size distribution of her vWF to classify the disease.
items.explanation: Step 1: a ratio **below 0.7** means a **qualitative (type 2)** defect. Step 2: to tell 2A (absent HMW multimers) from 2M (normal multimers), look at the **size distribution of vWF** — that is **multimer analysis**.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has new bruising. His APTT is prolonged and his PT is normal. The team needs to know whether this is a factor deficiency or a circulating inhibitor.
items.explanation: Step 1: an isolated prolonged APTT can come from a missing factor or an inhibitor. Step 2: mixing with normal plasma **corrects** a deficiency but **not** an inhibitor, so the **mixing study** answers the question.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman with type 2 VWD has reduced high-molecular-weight multimers. Her platelet count fell after desmopressin. The team wants to show that her vWF binds platelet GPIb abnormally strongly.
items.explanation: Step 1: low platelets after desmopressin plus reduced HMW multimers suggest **type 2B**. Step 2: the test of **GPIb binding** is **RIPA**, which is **enhanced** in 2B.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Plasma-derived factor VIII concentrate containing vWF

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman with type 1 von Willebrand disease needs a minor skin excision. A previous trial dose of a drug that releases endothelial vWF worked well.
items.explanation: Type 1 with a proven response: **desmopressin** for minor surgery.

items.stem: A 33-year-old man with type 3 von Willebrand disease is brought in after a road traffic collision with a large thigh haematoma.
items.explanation: Major bleeding in **type 3** (no releasable vWF) needs **vWF-containing factor VIII concentrate**.

items.stem: A 16-year-old girl with type 3 von Willebrand disease has a severe nosebleed in a remote hospital. No virus-inactivated or recombinant factor products are available.
items.explanation: Two steps: type 3 needs vWF replacement, and when virus-inactivated or recombinant products are unavailable, **cryoprecipitate** (which contains vWF and FVIII) is the fallback.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has a platelet count of 8 × 10⁹/L, widespread purpura and significant gum bleeding. The film is otherwise normal and the bone marrow shows plenty of megakaryocytes.
items.explanation: This is **ITP** with significant mucosal bleeding: **IV immunoglobulin** combined with **glucocorticoids**.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman with no previous bleeding history develops extensive bruising. Her APTT is prolonged and does not correct when mixed 1:1 with normal plasma. Factor VIII is low.
items.explanation: Two steps: failure to correct on mixing means an **inhibitor**, and the low FVIII identifies the target — an **acquired factor VIII inhibitor**.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has nosebleeds and heavy periods. The platelet count and PT are normal, the APTT is slightly prolonged, and both factor VIII and vWF are reduced.
items.explanation: Mucosal bleeding with **low vWF and low FVIII** is **VWD**; the APTT lengthens because of the FVIII fall.

items.stem: A 7-year-old girl, whose parents are first cousins, has severe nosebleeds. Platelet count and morphology are normal, vWF is normal, and her platelets fail to aggregate with ADP or collagen.
items.explanation: Normal count and morphology with **absent aggregation** and normal vWF is **Glanzmann thrombasthenia** (no GPIIb/IIIa), an autosomal recessive disorder.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Increased vWF affinity for platelet GPIb
Defective vWF binding of factor VIII
Uraemic impairment of platelet adhesion and aggregation

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with fever, confusion and a platelet count of 15 × 10⁹/L. The blood film shows fragmented red cells.
items.explanation: Encephalopathy, thrombocytopenia and MAHA suggest **TTP**: lack of **ADAMTS13** leaves ultralarge vWF multimers that form microthrombi.

items.stem: A 79-year-old man with an ejection systolic murmur and syncope on exertion has recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding from small-bowel vascular malformations. He has no previous bleeding history.
items.explanation: Two steps: the murmur and syncope point to severe **aortic stenosis**, and with GI bleeding this is **Heyde syndrome** — shear forces across the valve **cleave vWF**.

items.stem: A 14-year-old boy has lifelong mucosal bleeding. The film shows giant platelets and a mildly low count. His plasma vWF antigen and activity are normal.
items.explanation: Giant platelets and mild thrombocytopenia with normal plasma vWF mean the platelet **vWF receptor (GPIb-IX) is missing** — Bernard–Soulier syndrome.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has new petechiae and a platelet count of 12 × 10⁹/L. The film is otherwise normal and the marrow shows increased megakaryocytes.
items.explanation: Isolated thrombocytopenia with plentiful megakaryocytes is **ITP**, usually caused by **autoantibodies against GPIIb/IIIa**.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 20-year-old woman has mild mucosal bleeding and a platelet count of 110 × 10⁹/L. Ristocetin-induced platelet agglutination is enhanced, and high-molecular-weight vWF multimers are reduced.
items.explanation: **Enhanced RIPA**, reduced HMW multimers and **thrombocytopenia** together mean **type 2B**.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman has an APTT of 48 s and factor VIII:C of 15%. vWF antigen and ristocetin cofactor activity are normal. Her parents are first cousins with no bleeding history, and her brother has the same results.
items.explanation: Two steps: low FVIII in a **woman** whose brother is also affected and whose **parents are unaffected** points to **autosomal recessive** disease, not X-linked haemophilia. Normal vWF levels with low FVIII means vWF cannot carry FVIII — **type 2N**.

items.stem: A 3-year-old boy has a swollen knee after a minor fall. His maternal uncle had the same problem. His APTT is prolonged, PT is normal, and factor VIII and vWF levels are normal.
items.explanation: Two steps: a haemarthrosis in a boy with an affected **maternal uncle** suggests an **X-linked** factor deficiency (factor XI deficiency is autosomal). A prolonged APTT with **normal FVIII** then points to **haemophilia B** (factor IX).

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman has lifelong easy bruising and heavy periods; her mother and son are affected too. Platelet count, PT and APTT are normal. vWF antigen, ristocetin cofactor activity and factor VIII are all about 45%.
items.explanation: A **normal APTT does not exclude VWD**. Parallel moderate reductions with autosomal dominant spread fit **type 1**.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with mild von Willebrand disease needs a colonoscopic polypectomy. He has had a myocardial infarction and has peripheral arterial disease with claudication.
questions.leadIn: Which treatment should be avoided because of his medical history?
questions.explanation: **Desmopressin is contraindicated in severe arterial disease** because it can provoke thrombosis. Factor replacement or local measures are used instead.
whyNot: Tranexamic acid is a standard adjunct for mucosal bleeding in VWD; the arterial-disease contraindication in Davidson's applies to desmopressin.
vWF-containing FVIII concentrate is a standard alternative when desmopressin is unsuitable.
Recombinant vWF is an alternative replacement option, not a drug avoided for arterial disease.
Local measures are safe and treat many minor bleeds.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man has had three admissions for iron-deficiency anaemia from gastrointestinal bleeding. Capsule endoscopy shows small-bowel vascular malformations. He has a slow-rising pulse and an ejection systolic murmur. He has never had bleeding problems before, and vWF activity is now reduced.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely mechanism of his vWF abnormality?
options: Shear-induced cleavage of vWF across a stenotic aortic valve
Deficiency of the vWF-cleaving protease ADAMTS13
Reduced hepatic synthesis of factor VIII
questions.explanation: Aortic stenosis, GI bleeding from AVMs and acquired VWD make up **Heyde syndrome**. High shear forces across the narrowed valve **cleave and destroy vWF**.
whyNot: Inherited type 1 VWD would cause a lifelong history, but he has never bled before.
ADAMTS13 deficiency causes TTP, with ultralarge vWF multimers and thrombosis, not loss of vWF.
Anti-platelet antibodies cause ITP with thrombocytopenia, not reduced vWF activity.
Reduced hepatic factor synthesis occurs in liver disease and would not explain a new loss of vWF activity linked to valve disease.

ospe.identify: Stages of normal haemostasis: GPIa binds collagen, **GPIb binds vWF**, GPIIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen, then the fibrin clot forms. Be ready to point to the step VWD affects (adhesion).
Platelet structure: identify **GPIb/V/IX (the vWF receptor)**, GPIIb/IIIa (the fibrinogen receptor), GPIa/IIa (collagen) and the alpha and dense granules.
Factor VIII–vWF synthesis: normal, **haemophilia A** (X-linked FVIII gene defect, vWF normal) and **VWD** (low endothelial vWF, so FVIII is unprotected and falls).
